# Page 3^page=3
Query evaluation strategy A table Publications( PubCode, ISBN, Title, Date, ... ) has ISBN as candidate key (unique, not null) and stores 1.000.000 tuples. It is a hash-based structure, built on the primary key (PubCode), with: - 10 tuples per block - an average filling factor of 80% - an average lookup cost of 1.11 i/o operations An idea of the table: - 100.000 blocks in the primary hash structure (1M tuples, 10 tuples/block) - The lookup costs of 1.11 is a given, «measured» figure, that cannot be derived from the other parameters, so we… «trust» the measurement! But how can we «visualize» it? We can «imagine» that there is 10% probability that a bucket is full and requires reading one extra «overflow» block, 1% probability that the overflow requires reading 2 extra blocks, negligible probability that a fourth block is needed.… h(PubCode) 1M t 100K b 10 t/b

# Page 4^page=4
Query evaluation strategy First Question (scenario 1) a) Ignoring the possible effects of caching, and only taking account of disk i/o operations, estimate the execution cost of the query: select * from Publications where ( PubCode = 'ABC123' or PubCode = 'DEF456' ) and ISBN = '001122345'… h(PubCode) 1M t 100K b 10 t/b

# Page 5^page=5
At the outmost level of the where clause there is a conjunction of predicates. We have - one access structure that supports indexed access based on one predicate (PubCode) - no support for the other predicate (ISBN) so only the first conjunct can be used to retrieve the relevant tuple. Being in turn a disjunction, the second conjunct requires 2 accesses to the structure to be fully evaluated, at the (average) cost of 2.22 i/o operations.

# Page 6^page=6
Second Question (scenario 2) b) Assume that a secondary access structure is also available, in the form of a B+ tree index with ISBN as search key, with an average fan-out of 100. Still ignoring the impact of caching mechanisms, estimate the cost of execution through the secondary structure and compare the result with the previous one. select * from Publications where ( CodPubbl = 'ABC123‘ or CodPubbl = 'DEF456' ) and ISBN = '001122345'… h(PubCode) 1M t 100K b 10 t/b B+(ISBN)

# Page 7^page=7
Even if (optimistic assumption) the B+ tree is full and well-balanced, its depth cannot be less than 3, because log100106 = 3 Thus, each access to the index requires a minimum of 3 i/o ops just to reach a leaf node with the pointer to the primary storage (+1 access to actually retrieve the tuple). We conclude that the most convenient approach is still the previous strategy. Indeed, hash-based storage is hardly beatable for random access, whereas B+ trees excel with interval queries

# Page 9^page=9
A table T(Name,Surname,City,Pathology,BloodType) has 10.000.000 tuples and 3 multi-attribute indexes: Idx1(City,Name,Surname) Idx2(Pathlogy,Name,BloodType) Idx3(Pathology,Surname,City) The access keys are made by the listed attributes from left to right. All attributes have a (reasonably) uniform and independent distribution, with: val(Name) = 1000 val(City) = 1000 val(Pathology) = 100 val(Surname) = 2000 val(BloodType) = 10 Choice of the most effective index Choose the most convenient index to evaluate the query: select * from T where Name = "N" and Surname = "S" and Pathology = "P" and BloodType = "BT"
